prompt: What regiochemistry does hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene give?

choices.text: Non-Markovnikov: the −OH ends up on the less highly substituted carbon
Markovnikov: the −OH ends up on the more highly substituted carbon
choices.why: That is oxymercuration–demercuration. Hydroboration–oxidation is the complementary, non-Markovnikov method.

choices.text: No preference: a 50:50 mixture of both possible alcohols
choices.why: Hydroboration is regioselective: boron attaches to the less crowded carbon.

choices.text: Non-Markovnikov: the −H ends up on the less highly substituted carbon
choices.why: In this non-Markovnikov hydration, −H goes to the more substituted carbon and −OH to the less substituted one.

explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation complements oxymercuration–demercuration. Boron attaches to the less highly substituted carbon and is then replaced by −OH, giving the non-Markovnikov alcohol.

prompt: What two-step sequence carries out hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene?

choices.text: BH3 in THF, then H2O2 in basic solution
H2O2 in basic solution, then BH3 in THF
choices.why: Boron must add first to make the organoborane, which H2O2 then oxidizes.

choices.text: Hg(OAc)2 in aqueous THF, then NaBH4
choices.why: That is oxymercuration–demercuration, which gives the Markovnikov alcohol.

choices.text: BH3 in THF, then aqueous H2SO4
choices.why: The organoborane is oxidized with basic hydrogen peroxide, not treated with acid.

explanation: A B–H bond of borane, BH3, adds to the alkene to give an organoborane. Oxidation with basic hydrogen peroxide, H2O2 and OH−, then replaces boron with −OH to give the alcohol.

prompt: What happens when borane, BH3, is dissolved in tetrahydrofuran (THF)?

choices.text: It accepts an electron pair from THF, forming a stable BH3–THF complex
It donates an electron pair to a THF molecule, forming a complex
choices.why: Borane is the Lewis acid: it accepts an electron pair from the solvent; it doesn't donate one.

choices.text: It adds across a double bond in THF to give an organoborane
choices.why: THF is the solvent and has no C=C bond. BH3 forms a Lewis acid–base complex with it.

choices.text: It transfers H+ to a THF molecule, leaving behind a BH2− anion
choices.why: Borane acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair, not by giving up a proton.

explanation: Boron in BH3 has only six valence electrons. In THF solution, BH3 accepts an electron pair from a solvent molecule in a Lewis acid–base reaction, completing its octet and forming a stable BH3–THF complex.

prompt: How many electrons are in the valence shell of the boron atom in borane, BH3?
explanation: Boron has only six electrons in its valence shell in BH3, rather than an octet, which makes borane a very reactive Lewis acid. In THF it completes its octet by accepting an electron pair from a solvent molecule.

prompt: When an alkene reacts with BH3 in THF, addition to the double bond happens repeatedly. How many alkene molecules add to each BH3?
explanation: Rapid addition to the double bond occurs three times, giving a trialkylborane, R3B. For example, 1 molar equivalent of BH3 adds to 3 molar equivalents of cyclohexene to give tricyclohexylborane.

prompt: What forms when tricyclohexylborane is treated with H2O2 in basic solution?

choices.text: Three equivalents of cyclohexanol, plus boric acid
One equivalent of cyclohexanol, with two cyclohexyl groups left on boron
choices.why: All three C–B bonds are broken, so each cyclohexyl group becomes cyclohexanol.

choices.text: Three equivalents of cyclohexene
choices.why: Oxidation puts −OH on each carbon that was bonded to boron; it doesn't re-form the alkene.

choices.text: Three equivalents of cyclohexane
choices.why: The C–B bonds are replaced by C–OH bonds, not C–H bonds.

explanation: During oxidation the three C–B bonds are broken and −OH groups bond to the three carbons, giving 3 equivalents of cyclohexanol (87% yield) and boric acid. The net effect of hydroboration–oxidation is hydration of the double bond.

prompt: Assuming complete reaction, how many moles of cyclohexanol can be made from 0.50 mol of BH3 and excess cyclohexene by hydroboration–oxidation?
explanation: Each BH3 adds to three cyclohexene molecules to form tricyclohexylborane, and oxidation turns each of the three C–B bonds into a C–OH. So 0.50 mol BH3 × 3 = 1.5 mol cyclohexanol.

prompt: What is the product of hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclopentene?

choices.text: trans-2-Methylcyclopentanol
cis-2-Methylcyclopentanol
choices.why: H and B add to the same face, and −OH replaces B with the same stereochemistry, which leaves the methyl and −OH on opposite faces.

choices.text: 1-Methylcyclopentanol
choices.why: That is the Markovnikov product from oxymercuration–demercuration. Boron attaches to the less substituted carbon.

choices.text: A 50:50 mixture of cis- and trans-2-methylcyclopentanol
choices.why: Syn addition in a single step gives only the trans product.

explanation: Boron and hydrogen add syn, with boron on the less substituted carbon, and oxidation replaces boron with −OH with the same stereochemistry. The new H and the −OH are on the same face, so the methyl is pushed to the other face: trans-2-methylcyclopentanol, in 85% yield.

prompt: Boron and hydrogen add to an alkene with syn stereochemistry. What does syn mean?

choices.text: Both add from the same face of the double bond
They add from opposite faces of the double bond
choices.why: That is anti stereochemistry, as in Br2 addition.

choices.text: Both add to the same carbon
choices.why: Boron bonds to one double-bond carbon and hydrogen to the other.

choices.text: Boron adds to the more highly substituted carbon
choices.why: That would describe regiochemistry, not stereochemistry, and boron actually goes to the less substituted carbon.

explanation: Syn stereochemistry, the opposite of anti, means both groups add from the same face. In hydroboration the C–H and C–B bonds form at the same time on the same face of the alkene.

prompt: How does the mechanism of hydroboration differ from many other alkene additions?

choices.text: It occurs in a single step, without a carbocation intermediate
It goes through a cyclic boron-bridged cation, like a bromonium ion
choices.why: No intermediate forms; the C–H and C–B bonds form at the same time.

choices.text: It goes through the more substituted carbocation
choices.why: There is no carbocation in hydroboration.

choices.text: It goes through radical intermediates
choices.why: Hydroboration occurs in a single step, with no intermediate of any kind.

explanation: Hydroboration occurs in a single step in which the C–H and C–B bonds form at the same time and on the same face of the double bond. With no carbocation involved, the result is syn addition.

prompt: Why does hydroboration give non-Markovnikov regiochemistry?

choices.text: Boron bonds to the less crowded carbon, via the lower-energy transition state
Boron attaches to the carbon that gives the more stable carbocation
choices.why: No carbocation forms in hydroboration; steric crowding decides where boron goes.

choices.text: H2O2 moves the −OH to the less substituted carbon during oxidation
choices.why: −OH takes boron's place with the same stereochemistry. The regiochemistry is set when boron adds.

choices.text: BH3 acts as a Lewis base and attacks the more positive carbon
choices.why: BH3 is a Lewis acid. Its regiochemistry comes from steric crowding.

explanation: Attachment of boron is favored at the less sterically crowded carbon of the alkene. The transition state with less steric crowding is lower in energy and forms faster (Figure 8.5.1), leading to non-Markovnikov regiochemistry.

prompt: In the oxidation step of hydroboration–oxidation, how does −OH replace boron?

choices.text: At the same carbon, with the same stereochemistry
At the same carbon, but on the opposite face from boron
choices.why: The −OH takes boron's place with the same stereochemistry, keeping the syn result.

choices.text: At the neighboring carbon
choices.why: −OH bonds to the carbon that held boron; that's why the alcohol is non-Markovnikov.

choices.text: At the same carbon, on either face at random
choices.why: The replacement keeps boron's stereochemistry, so a single product forms.

explanation: During oxidation, boron is replaced by −OH with the same stereochemistry. Together with the syn addition of H and B, that gives an overall syn, non-Markovnikov addition of water.

prompt: What alcohol would you expect from hydroboration–oxidation of 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2?

choices.text: 2-Methyl-1-propanol, (CH3)2CHCH2OH
2-Methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3COH
choices.why: That's the Markovnikov alcohol. Boron, and then −OH, goes to the less crowded CH2 carbon.

choices.text: 1-Butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH
choices.why: Hydration doesn't change the carbon skeleton; the branch stays.

choices.text: 2-Methyl-1,2-propanediol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2OH
choices.why: Hydroboration–oxidation adds one H and one OH, not two OH groups.

explanation: Boron attaches to the less sterically crowded CH2 carbon and H to the more substituted carbon. Oxidation replaces boron with −OH, giving (CH3)2CHCH2OH, 2-methyl-1-propanol: the non-Markovnikov product.

prompt: 2-Methyl-2-pentene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3, is hydrated two ways: (a) BH3, then H2O2, OH−; (b) Hg(OAc)2, H2O, then NaBH4. Which pair of products is correct?

choices.text: (a) 2-methyl-3-pentanol; (b) 2-methyl-2-pentanol
(a) 2-methyl-2-pentanol; (b) 2-methyl-3-pentanol
choices.why: This is reversed. Hydroboration gives the non-Markovnikov alcohol; oxymercuration gives the Markovnikov alcohol.

choices.text: (a) 2-methyl-3-pentanol; (b) 2-methyl-3-pentanol
choices.why: The two methods are complementary and give different alcohols.

choices.text: (a) 2-methyl-2-pentanol; (b) 2-methyl-2-pentanol
choices.why: Hydroboration puts −OH on the less substituted carbon, carbon 3, so the two products differ.

explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation is syn and non-Markovnikov, putting −OH on carbon 3: 2-methyl-3-pentanol. Oxymercuration–demercuration is Markovnikov, putting −OH on carbon 2: 2-methyl-2-pentanol (Worked Example 8.1).

prompt: What is the best way to prepare 4-methyl-3-hexanol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH2CH3, from an alkene?

choices.text: Hydroboration–oxidation of 3-methyl-3-hexene
Hydroboration–oxidation of 4-methyl-2-hexene
choices.why: Its double bond is disubstituted (RCH=CHR′), so it would probably give a mixture of two alcohols.

choices.text: Oxymercuration–demercuration of 3-methyl-3-hexene
choices.why: Markovnikov addition would put −OH on the methyl-bearing carbon, giving 3-methyl-3-hexanol.

choices.text: Hydroboration–oxidation of 3-methyl-2-hexene
choices.why: That would put −OH on carbon 2, giving 3-methyl-2-hexanol.

explanation: Work backward: the −OH-bearing carbon must have been a double-bond carbon, so the candidates are 4-methyl-2-hexene and 3-methyl-3-hexene. The first is disubstituted and would give a mixture. 3-Methyl-3-hexene is trisubstituted, and non-Markovnikov hydroboration puts −OH on its less substituted carbon, giving only the desired alcohol (Worked Example 8.2).

prompt: Why would 4-methyl-2-hexene, CH3CH=CHCH(CH3)CH2CH3, probably give a mixture of two alcohols with either hydration method?

choices.text: Its double bond is disubstituted, RCH=CHR′, so neither carbon is favored
Its double bond is at the end of the chain, so both ends react
choices.why: Its double bond is between carbons 2 and 3, not at the end of the chain.

choices.text: Its double bond is tetrasubstituted, so both carbons are too crowded
choices.why: Each double-bond carbon carries one alkyl group and one H, so it's disubstituted.

choices.text: Both methods form a carbocation that can be attacked from either end
choices.why: Hydroboration involves no carbocation. The mixture arises because both double-bond carbons are equally substituted.

explanation: 4-Methyl-2-hexene has a disubstituted double bond, RCH=CHR′. Markovnikov's rule does not apply to symmetrically substituted alkenes, so either method would probably give a mixture of 4-methyl-2-hexanol and 4-methyl-3-hexanol.

prompt: What alkene could be used to prepare 3-methyl-2-butanol, CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)2, by hydroboration–oxidation?

choices.text: 2-Methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3
3-Methyl-1-butene, CH2=CHCH(CH3)2
choices.why: Hydroboration would put −OH on the terminal CH2, giving 3-methyl-1-butanol.

choices.text: 2-Methyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3
choices.why: Hydroboration would put −OH on the CH2 carbon, giving 2-methyl-1-butanol.

choices.text: 1-Pentene, CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3
choices.why: It lacks the methyl branch, and hydration doesn't change the carbon skeleton.

explanation: In 2-methyl-2-butene, the CH carbon is less substituted than the carbon bearing two methyls. Hydroboration puts boron, then −OH, on that CH, giving (CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3, 3-methyl-2-butanol.

prompt: What alkene would you hydroborate and oxidize to make cyclohexylmethanol, C6H11CH2OH?

choices.text: Methylenecyclohexane, C6H10=CH2
1-Methylcyclohexene
choices.why: Hydroboration would put −OH on the ring carbon next to the methyl, giving trans-2-methylcyclohexanol.

choices.text: Cyclohexene
choices.why: That has only six carbons; the product needs a seventh, the CH2OH carbon.

choices.text: Cyclohexylethylene, C6H11CH=CH2
choices.why: That has eight carbons and would give 2-cyclohexylethanol.

explanation: In methylenecyclohexane, the =CH2 carbon is the less crowded one. Boron, and then −OH, attaches there, giving C6H11CH2OH, cyclohexylmethanol.

prompt: What alcohol forms from hydroboration–oxidation of ethylidenecyclohexane, in which a ring carbon of cyclohexane is double-bonded to a CHCH3 group?

choices.text: 1-Cyclohexylethanol, C6H11CH(OH)CH3
1-Ethylcyclohexanol
choices.why: That is the Markovnikov product, with −OH on the ring carbon. Boron goes to the less crowded CH carbon.

choices.text: 2-Cyclohexylethanol, C6H11CH2CH2OH
choices.why: The −OH must go on a former double-bond carbon, and the CH3 carbon wasn't one.

choices.text: 2-Ethylcyclohexanol
choices.why: That puts −OH on a ring carbon that wasn't part of the double bond.

explanation: The ring carbon carries two ring bonds and is the more substituted end of the double bond; the CH is less crowded. Boron, then −OH, attaches to that CH, giving C6H11CH(OH)CH3, 1-cyclohexylethanol.

prompt: Hydroboration–oxidation of 1,4-dimethylcyclopentene gives a mixture of two alcohols rather than one. What is the reason?

choices.text: Syn addition can occur on either face, and the carbon-4 methyl makes the faces differ
Boron adds to either double-bond carbon, giving Markovnikov and non-Markovnikov alcohols
choices.why: Boron goes to the less substituted carbon, so both alcohols are non-Markovnikov.

choices.text: The addition is anti on one face of the ring but syn on the other face
choices.why: Hydroboration is always syn: H and B add from the same face in a single step.

choices.text: A carbocation forms, and water attacks it from either face of the ring
choices.why: Hydroboration occurs in one step with no carbocation.

explanation: Boron always adds to the less substituted carbon, with H and B on the same face, and −OH replaces B with the same stereochemistry, so in each product the −OH is trans to the neighboring methyl. But the addition can happen on the face nearer the carbon-4 methyl or on the opposite face, giving two different 2,4-dimethylcyclopentanols.
